extracted.intended_audience: higher-education administrators, policymakers, accreditation professionals, and academics concerned with quality in online/distance learning
extracted.subtask_short: quality frameworks for online higher education
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes criteria, benchmarks, and standards used across jurisdictions to evaluate or design quality assurance for online and distance higher education. Includes institutional, programmatic, consumer-facing, and benchmarking dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Australian self-accrediting quality assurance expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: To be 'self-accrediting,' universities must demonstrate that they have appropriate quality assurance procedures in place; 'universities are expected to engage in a pro-active, rigorous and ongoing process of planning and self-assessment which will enable them to ensure the quality outcomes expected by their students and the wider community' (DETYA, 2000, p.17).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on institutional planning, ongoing self-assessment, and demonstrable procedures. Connected to national qualification frameworks that communicate expected standards for each level of post-secondary achievement and intended to signal attractiveness to employers/investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: QAA features of academic review
rubrics_metrics.description: The 2004 QAA handbook describes academic review features including: a focus on the students' learning experience; peer review; flexibility of process to minimise disruption; a process conducted in an atmosphere of mutual trust (reviewers do not normally expect to find areas for improvement the college has not identified); emphasis on maintenance and enhancement of academic standards and engagement with academic infrastructure; use of self-evaluation as the key document (reflective and evaluative focus); onus on the college to provide all relevant information; and evidence-based judgements. (QAA, 2004b, p.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review processes should privilege student learning experience, peer judgement, institution-led self-evaluation, evidence-based findings, and minimising disruption. Reviewers generally expect institutions to identify their own improvement areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: QAA Codes of Practice (ten areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: QAA developed Codes of Practice covering ten areas: postgraduate research programs; collaborative provision and flexible and distributed learning (including e-learning); students with disabilities; external examining; assessment of students; program approval, monitoring and review; career education, information and guidance; placement learning; recruitment; and admissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Codes provide sector-specific good-practice expectations across core academic and student lifecycle functions; intended to integrate distance/e-learning concerns with broader academic quality standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: QAA distance learning guideline elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The first iteration of QAA distance learning guidelines included five system design elements; six elements for academic standards, program design and approval; three on management of delivery; one on student development and support; three on student communication and representation; and five on student assessment. The 2004 revision encompasses good practices for delivery options which 'in general do not require the student to attend particular classes or events at particular times and particular locations' (QAA, 2004a, p.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidelines stress integration between distance delivery and general teaching/learning quality standards; they enumerate specific elements across design, standards, management, support, communication, and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: ODLQC accreditation standard sections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Open and Distance Learning Quality Council (ODLQC) accreditation standards are organized in six sections: outcomes (9 standards); resources (4 standards); support (7 standards); selling (9 standards); providers (10 standards); and collaborative provision (5 standards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards are tilt toward institutional/process issues. The sections cover learner outcomes, institutional resourcing, student support, marketing/sales practices, provider responsibilities, and arrangements with collaborators.

rubrics_metrics.name: ODLQC Buyers Guide questions (consumer-facing criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: ODLQC produced a Buyers Guide listing questions prospective students should ask: e.g., course questions — 'Can you look at the course first? Is the course right for you? How much support does it offer? Is there face-to-face training? Can you talk to former students? Have previous learners been successful? Can you compare courses?'; outcomes questions — 'What do you want to achieve? Is this the right qualification? Will there be an exam at the end? Are there restrictions?'; cost questions — 'How much will it cost? Is financial support available? When can you get your money back?'; quality — 'Is the provider independently inspected/accredited?' (ODLQC, 2003, p.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Buyer-oriented checklist for course selection. Warns that alternative quality marks (e.g., ISO) may suggest quality but 'do not guarantee it.' Useful both for consumers and as transparency expectations for providers.

rubrics_metrics.name: CVCP proposed elements for borderless education quality frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: For borderless education the proposed framework would include: currency and security of qualifications; audit of the system for design and approval of curricula or appropriate learning contracts; an internationally recognized system of educational credit; licensing of staff; security of assessment; adequate and accurate public information about learning opportunities; approved guidance and complaints systems for learners; transparent quality management processes for each agent in the educational supply chain; access to learning resources assured by the provider; and publication of guidance relevant to different modes of provision. (CVCP, 2000, p.30).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targets cross-border and commercial providers: focuses on credential integrity, curricular approval systems, assessment security, consumer information and complaints, staff licensing, and transparency across the supply chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canadian Recommended e-Learning Guidelines (CanREGS) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: CanREGS comprises 138 recommendations organized into three sections: Quality Outcomes from e-Learning Products and Services (15 items on how students acquire content skills, knowledge, and learning skills); Quality Processes and Practices (20 items on management of students and delivery using appropriate technologies); and Quality Inputs and Resources (103 items spanning intended learning outcomes, curriculum content, materials, product/service information, learning technologies, technical design, personnel, learning resources, evaluation, program plans/budgets, advertising, recruitment, and admissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comprehensive, consumer-oriented, consensus-based and adaptable; includes exhaustive inputs/resources checklist—acknowledges not all guidelines apply to all circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer's Guide to e-Learning (Canadian) questions and institutional adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer guide structures 34 questions into basic, discerning, and detailed levels for students (examples: 'What is my purpose for taking this course? Do I need a credit or certificate? How much can I afford? What hardware/software do I have? Where will I access the Internet? Are my computer skills adequate? Will I need technical help?'). Adapted institutional questions include: 'What is our purpose for offering this course? Do we know what we expect students to learn? Do we have the technological infrastructure? How skilled are our course developers and instructors? What technical assistance do we have available?'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps both consumers choose courses and institutions audit readiness; encourages reframing consumer questions into institutional planning checklists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of Commitment values for electronically offered programs (regional accreditors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional accrediting commissions declared values: education best experienced within a community of learning with competent professionals; learning is dynamic and interactive regardless of setting; integrity of degree programs organized around substantive and coherent curricula defining expected learning outcomes; institutions accept obligation to address student needs and provide necessary resources; institutions responsible for education provided in their name; institutions undertake assessment and improvement of quality with emphasis on student learning; institutions voluntarily subject themselves to peer review. (reprinted in Eaton, 2002, p.26).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles for evaluating electronically offered degrees: focus on community, interactivity, coherent curricula, resource commitment, institutional responsibility, continual assessment/improvement, and peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: WCET 'Best Practices' sections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Western Cooperative for Educational Telecommunications Best Practices are organized into five sections: institutional context and commitment; curriculum and instruction; faculty support; student support; and evaluation and assessment (WCET, n.d.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework for institution-level review and continuous improvement of electronically delivered programs emphasizing support structures and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phipps & Merisotis 'Quality on the Line' essential benchmarks (24)
rubrics_metrics.description: From an initial list of 45 possible benchmarks the study identified 24 considered 'essential' to ensure quality in Internet-based distance education. Categories include institutional support, course development, teaching and learning, course structure, student support, faculty support, and evaluation and assessment benchmarks (see Table 4, Appendix A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended as benchmarks institutions should consider essential; used to compare recognition across institutions and stakeholder perceptions of importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: ACODE benchmarking components and eight prioritized areas
rubrics_metrics.description: ACODE pilot framework components: institutional context, purpose, scope, principles of service delivery, benchmarking priorities, indicators for priority areas, self-assessment/ranking, comparative matrix of strengths/weaknesses, and action plan for self-improvement. The full articulation of benchmarks includes scoping statements, a good-practice statement, performance indicators, and performance measures (ratings) in eight areas: (1) institutional policy and governance for technology-supported learning and teaching; (2) planning for, and quality improvement of the integration of technologies for learning and teaching; (3) information technology infrastructure to support learning and teaching; (4) pedagogical application of information and communication technology; (5) professional/staff development for effective use of technologies; (6) staff support for use of technologies; (7) student training for effective use of technologies; (8) student support for use of technologies (ACODE, 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmarking process involves scoring planning, development, and implementation stages across elements; includes scoping, indicators, self-ranking and action planning to drive improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarking approach with process levels and domain granularity (New Zealand example)
rubrics_metrics.description: A New Zealand project scored five process levels (delivery, planning, definition, management, and optimization) against 35 standards. Domains investigated included: ten factors for processes with impacts on learning; seven factors on development of e-learning resources; six factors related to student and operational support; three factors related to evaluation and quality controls; and nine factors related to institutional planning and management (Marshall, 2006).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates applying software-development style granularity and maturity/process-level scoring to e-learning quality; useful when detailed operational benchmarking is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on process integrity over simplistic outcome/inputs measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique that institutional reputation, resources, and student/alumni outcomes are 'potentially quite misleading' and often driven by inputs rather than effective educational practices; solution should rest in careful measures addressing the integrity of teaching and learning processes within institutions (Pascarella, 2001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages development of measures that capture teaching/learning integrity and warns against naive reliance on easily measured but potentially invalid input/output proxies; supports process-focused benchmarks and evidence of pedagogical effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained institutional commitment to support distance learners
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring theme: institutions must demonstrate sustained commitment—long-term planned infrastructure development, investment in technical systems, and training for support and instructional staff—instead of treating online delivery as experimental one-offs. Student support should be determined by program nature and student needs to enable reasonable chances of attainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmarks should include evidence of long-term infrastructure planning, staff development programs, and reliable student support systems; one-off or short-cycle technology investments are cautioned against.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of learning technologies to enable effective learning characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning technologies should 'enable the identified characteristics of effective learning environments and ensure that they are present and accessible' and should mobilize recent theory and research into how people learn to enhance learning (Herrington et al., 2001, p.266).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality assessment should examine how technologies support learning design principles, accessibility, interaction, context, and community; technology alone is insufficient without alignment to learning theory and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer/league-table and web-based ranking metrics (OEDb/COOL-derived)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumer-facing ranking metrics used by Online Education Database (OEDb) and derived from Department of Education sources include: accreditation by recognized bodies; acceptance rates; financial aid availability; retention and graduation rates; peer web citations (Yahoo link domain search); scholarly citations (Google Scholar); student-faculty ratio; years accredited (Peterson's); and, for predominantly-online institutions, digesting available data for institutions offering >=50% programs online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These metrics are often used by web directories and ranking sites for consumer comparison; they emphasize measurable institutional outcomes and web visibility but may not capture pedagogical quality or student learning processes.
